newsitem.title: ROMANIA: King Michael to lobby for Romania early NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: King Michael to lobby for Romania early NATO entry.

text.p: Romania's exiled King Michael will use his prestige to promote Romania's bid to win an early entry to NATO, President Emil Constantinescu said on Tuesday.
"I asked his majesty to advocate Romania's interests before the leaders of NATO members in Europe, especially before constitutional monarchies," Constantinescu told reporters.
He made the remarks after talks with King Michael, who visits his homeland shortly after the new centrist government restored his citizenship last month.
"I will do all what I can to help Romania," said Michael, who also attended Constantinescu's meeting with the press.
Constantinescu hailed the meeting with the country's former king as historic and marking Romania's return to "normality".
The meeting, a highlight of the six-day visit paid by Michael to his native country, took place at the Cotroceni presidential palace, a former royal residence.

Michael was forced to abdicate by pro-Moscow communists in 1947, three years after he broke an alliance with Nazi Germany and shifted his country's allegiance to the Allies. The ex-communists also stripped Michael of his Romanian citizenship and banned him from returning to his country.
Michael was greeted on Bucharest streets after his arrival last Friday from exile in Switzerland by 20,000 well-wishers.
The authorities and many Romanians view the visit as another sign that the country is returning to normal after seven years of post-communist uncertainty.

Constantinescu said he was confident the king, the only surviving World War Two head of state, could put to good use his prestige when presenting Romania's democratic achievements and its bid to enter NATO in the first wave of a planned enlargement expected to be announced at a NATO summit in July.
Over the past months Romania has intensified its diplomatic efforts to be promoted alongside Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, viewed as favourites in the race to join NATO.
During his visit, officially described as private, Michael also met Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea and several members of his cabinet.

Ex-communist Ion Iliescu, president from Ceausescu's 1989 demise until his election defeat last November, had blocked Michael's attempts to return home over the past five years and insisted he be treated as a foreign commoner.
